entries.title: Free Ink is an open source project for e-reader OS
entries.summary: Free Ink is an active, open-source collective dedicated to building a completely open e-reader ecosystem that spans software, firmware, and hardware. The post Free Ink is an open source project for e-reader OS first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Free Ink is an open-source collective building the software, firmware, and hardware for e-paper readers.. Community-built, fully open-source firmware for budget e-paper readers, with more features, more control, and an open base anyone can build on. It currently supports Xteink X4, Xteink X3, de-link, LilyGo T5 S3, Sticky, and M5Paper v1.1.

Free Ink parses EPUB 2 and 3, applies embedded CSS, and lays out chapters in your font, size, and margins. Pages are cached to SD on first open, so every reopen is near-instant. Noto Serif and Noto Sans built in, plus any font loaded from your SD card. Tune size, spacing, margins, hyphenation, alignment, and anti-aliasing. The reader runs an upload server over WiFi. Drop EPUBs in from any browser, send straight from Calibre, and keep your place across devices with KOReader sync. Full right-to-left layout for Hebrew and Arabic, plus translated menus in Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Ukrainian, Polish and more.

Not only is several e-readers fully supported, but the company has a software framework on GitHub that allows developers, hackers, tinkers and brands to experiment on their own hardware.

Michael Kozlowski has written about audiobooks, e-books and e-readers for the past eighteen years. He Lives in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.

entries.title: reTerminal Sticky is a tiny E INK, AI-powered magnetic display
entries.summary: Sticky is a 3.97-inch AI-powered magnetic ePaper display that keeps your family connected through visible notes, weather updates, and thoughtful messages. The post reTerminal Sticky is a tiny E INK, AI-powered magnetic display first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The reTerminal Sticky is an AI-powered magnetic e‑paper note device developed by Seeed Studio, designed specifically as a dedicated shared reminder screen for households. Instead of keeping reminders buried in a phone, Sticky makes important notes, to-dos, and warm family messages visible in places like the fridge, kitchen, hallway, or entryway. It is available on September 15th and retails for $49.99 on the Sticky Website.

Sticky features a crisp 3.4-inch E-Ink touchscreen with a resolution of 800 x 480. It is packed into a compact 4.5-inch outer frame. Users press an onboard physical button to speak, and the device instantly transcribes voice into notes or to-do lists. Built with an integrated magnetic backing and an extra adhesive magnetic ring for toolless mounting to refrigerators or non-metal walls. The e-paper screen lets the device run up to a week on a single charge under normal use, or months in Battery Saver Mode via the 750 mAh battery.

Use the Seeedash mobile App to manage your devices remotely and update content on the fly. Add a reminder or leave a surprise photo – all from your phone, and it shows up on the Sticky instantly for your family to see. For more creative control, use Seeedash Web to customize and deploy your content. Stay connected even when you’re miles away, however it only has a paltry 32MB of storage, but does have an SD card capable of 32GB.

People who just want to buy the device and use it normally can do so. However, it has a tremendous open source community behind it. It runs on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller with full open-source development tool chains. The community actively utilizes the device via ESPHome and custom OpenDisplay firmware to link it directly into Home Assistant. This allows developers to use the E-ink touch interface for smart home automations like room-by-room light controls. Supports flashing dedicated SenseCraft Human-Machine Interface firmware to deploy custom dashboard designs easily. It is fully compatible with CrossPoint, to turn the Sticky into an e-reader.

Michael Kozlowski has written about audiobooks, e-books and e-readers for the past eighteen years. He Lives in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.

entries.title: What is better, the Kindle Scribe 2024 or the Kindle Scribe 2025?
entries.summary: The 3rd Generation Amazon Kindle Scribe features an expanded 11-inch E Ink Oxide display, a thinner 5.4 mm profile, a lighter 400g build, and a faster quad-core processor with 12ms writing latency. In contrast, the 2nd Generation Scribe uses a 10.2-inch screen, a thicker asymmetrical bezel layout, and an older processor stack. The post What is better, the Kindle Scribe 2024 or the Kindle Scribe 20
entries.content:
The 2025 Kindle Scribe (3rd Generation) introduces a completely redesigned exterior, a larger display, and faster processing capabilities compared to the 2024 model. The 2025 version supports cloud storage providers such as Microsoft OneDrive and Google Drive, and it also includes several new AI features.

Kindle Scribe 2025 and 2026

  • Performance & Writing: The 2025 model runs on a snappier processor, creating a faster user interface and noticeably lower writing latency
  • Screen Clarity vs. Texture: The 2025 monochrome screen offers a whiter background and crisper text clarity. However, some users note this smoother screen layer slightly reduces the gritty, paper-like friction felt when writing on the 2024 version.
  • Smarter Software: The 2025 model includes new AI-powered tools that make searching notes smarter and more intuitive. This lets you type searches to instantly pull up handwritten notes.
  • Universal Note Search: Enter loose keywords into the main top search bar to index your cursive and print handwriting. The Kindle locates matching terms globally across your stored notebooks and identifies exact page numbers
  • Send to Alexa: is a feature that works with the user’s notes written on the Kindle Scribe and Scribe Colorsoft. Users can submit their notebooks or documents to the AI, which will then help with brainstorming new ideas, guidance for projects, or turning your notes into to-do lists.
  • Color Variant: Amazon expanded the 2025 lineup to include the premium Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for users wanting color highlights and document viewing.
  • Ask Notebooks: is a built-in generative AI search feature on the Kindle Scribe. It lets you search handwritten text, uncover insights, and ask conversational follow-up questions directly about your notebooks.
  • AI Reading Tools: Access upcoming reading companions like “Story So Far” for spoiler-free series catch-ups and “Ask This Book” to clear up narrative confusion as you read.
  • Larger Screen, Smaller Body: The screen footprint is increased from 10.2 inches to 11 inches while shrinking the bezels. This configuration gives you more writing space without expanding the tablet’s physical size.

Kindle Scribe 2024

The 2024 Kindle Scribe refresh introduces several hardware refinements, distinct visual styling, and the debut of built-in generative AI tools. It serves as a middle-ground upgrade focusing on a premium tactile feel and focused productivity.

  • Uniform White Borders: The device ditches asymmetric bezels for a clean, flush-front display surrounded by uniform white borders.
  • Paper-Like Screen Micro-Texture: The 300 PPI glare-free screen features an altered surface coating. This design gives the pen tip extra “bite” and friction to closely mimic real paper.
  • Upgraded Premium Pen: The standard bundle includes a re-weighted Premium Pen. It features a customizable shortcut button and a soft-tipped eraser that behaves like a traditional pencil.
  • Premium Color Options: The aluminum chassis comes in Metallic Jade and Tungsten finishes.
  • AI Note Summarization: Long, handwritten brainstorms or meeting minutes can be compressed into a bulleted summary directly on the device.
  • Active Canvas: When writing in a standard Kindle book, your stylus strokes dynamically move the layout. The software side panels expand automatically to fit your notes without burying the underlying text.

Wrap Up

The Kindle Scribe 3rd generation, Kindle Scribe Colorsoft, and Kindle Scribe without Front-Light are all models that have a ton of AI features, but tend to run on the more expensive side. The screen quality is better and larger than the 2024 model, and the screen has better resistance to drawing with the pen.

The Kindle Scribe 2024 model is good enough for most people and perfect for those who don’t use AI enhancements. This iteration of the Scribe is good enough for people who want to freehand draw, read Kindle books on a very large screen, and draw inside of them too. This is likely the most affordable Kindle Scribe, which also regularly goes on sale.

Like-New Amazon Kindle Scribe (16GB) - Your notes, documents and books, all in one place. With...

  • Like-New Amazon Kindle Scribe 16GB is refurbished, tested, and certified to look and work like new and comes with the same limited warranty as a new device. Like-New Amazon devices may be packaged in generic Amazon-branded boxes.
  • Kindle Scribe - A Kindle and a notebook, all in one. Redesigned flush-front display with uniform white borders and upgraded Premium Pen, feels like writing on paper.
  • Write in books – Start writing on the page and Active Canvas will create space for your notes. Expand the margins to add more notes, or collapse them to see the original page.

Amazon Kindle Scribe (16GB) - Your notes, documents and books, all in one place. With built-in AI...

  • A digital notebook for all your writing needs - Replace your stack of notebooks with a single device purpose-built for writing, reading, and thinking. No notifications or social media.
  • With AI tools to transform your notes - Convert messy handwriting into readable font, summarize your notes, and change their length and tone with built-in AI notebook tools.
  • Feels like pen on paper - See, feel and hear your thoughts meet the page with every stroke of the Premium Pen. No need to set up or charge, just start writing.

Amazon Kindle Scribe 32GB (newest model) — 11” paper-like display with front light — One...

  • All-new Kindle Scribe – Features an 11” glare-free display with front light, built-in notebook, AI tools, and support for popular cloud services.
  • Feels just like paper – Textured surface and ultra-fast responsiveness for a natural writing experience. Included Premium Pen requires no charging.
  • Thinner, lighter, faster – At just 5.4mm thin and 400g light, it's redesigned for comfort, with a larger 11” display, and 40% faster writing and page turns.

entries.title: Instapaper 10 brings tons of new features to iOS
entries.summary: Instapaper 10 is the biggest update to the iOS application in over a decade, introducing a comprehensive design overhaul alongside major feature updates. The post Instapaper 10 brings tons of new features to iOS first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Instapaper 10 is the biggest update to the iOS application in over a decade, introducing a comprehensive design overhaul alongside major feature updates. Released in late July 2026, the milestone release modernizes the save-for-later reading environment and accompanies a fully rebuilt web platform and new Android capabilities. “Instapaper 10 is our biggest update to the iOS app in over a decade. It’s a large redesign that adopts Liquid Glass, along with several new features and performance improvements.

Instapaper 10 is our biggest update to the iOS app in over a decade. It’s a large redesign that adopts Liquid Glass, along with several new features and performance improvements.

Section Counts: All sections now display a count of the articles or notes they contain. If section counts feel more anxiety-inducing than helpful, you can turn them off in Settings > Behavior > Section Counts.



Section Sorting: To sort your Folders or Tags, tap the “…” menu next to the section header and choose your preferred sort option.



Article List Appearance: They introduced Condensed View, new typography and styles, and an easy way to adjust the article list’s appearance. From an article list, tap “…”, then tap “Appearance” to adjust styles, fonts, and image thumbnails.

New Reading Fonts: They are introducing four new reading fonts in this release, two serifs and two sans-serifs: Literata, New York, Open Sans, and Atkinson Hyperlegible.

Home Screen Widget: Last but not least, we’re excited to launch a Home Screen widget for iOS. It displays your in-progress article and your most recently saved articles, and provides a one-tap shortcut to start reading your Instapaper saves.

They improved iPad multitasking, redesigned onboarding, made background syncing more reliable, and reduced article download times in this release. Together, these changes make this the fastest and best version of Instapaper for iOS yet.

Platform-Wide Ecosystem Improvements: Rebuilt Website: Accompanied by the mobile launch, the web version of Instapaper received its second-ever full platform rebuild since its original launch in 2008.

Android AI Voices: The Android app rebuilt its text-to-speech architecture from scratch to officially integrate premium, natural AI narration.

entries.title: Dasung Link 2 Review – A Smartphone Monitor
entries.summary: The Dasung Link 2 is a specialized 6.7-inch portable E-Ink smartphone monitor designed to reduce eye strain by mirroring your phone’s display onto a paper-like, glare-free surface. The post Dasung Link 2 Review – A Smartphone Monitor first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Dasung Link 2 is a specialized 6.7-inch portable E-Ink smartphone monitor designed to reduce eye strain by mirroring your phone’s display onto a paper-like, glare-free surface. It is not a standalone phone; it lacks its own processor, cellular radio, and operating system, meaning it completely relies on your connected smartphone’s hardware and apps to function.

The Dasung Link 2 features a 6.7-inch monochrome E-Ink display with a pixel density of 300 PPI. This crisp resolution mimics the reading quality of premium e-readers, ensuring text is incredibly sharp and easy on the eyes. It utilizes ambient light reflection and includes an adjustable dual-tone front light for comfortable night reading.

The Link 2 is equipped with DASUNG’s signature high-speed refresh technology operating at 60Hz, enabling fluid scrolling, typing, and video playback that closely mimic those of a standard LCD screen, with minimal ghosting. It uses wireless screen mirroring to broadcast displays seamlessly from both iOS and Android devices. Enables you to control your smartphone directly by tapping and swiping on the E-Ink screen itself.

The device is built with an ultra-thin, lightweight metal body featuring multi-function physical keys for easy image enhancement and contrast adjustments. It is also compatible with magnetic power banks for convenient outdoor use. The monitor does not contain an internal battery to keep it lightweight. Instead, it features dual USB-C ports and is typically powered by an external source.

It is important to note that the Link 2 inherits your phone’s CPU, RAM, and app performance to work properly. It is compatible with Android 12 and later, as well as modern versions of iOS and HarmonyOS. It retails for $329 from the Dasung website for the battery-free version or $349 for the battery variant. Space Grey and Glacier Blue are the two available colors.

entries.title: How to monitor e-book prices without losing half your data to failed requests
entries.summary: Learn how to monitor e-book prices across Kindle, Kobo and Apple Books with stable per-region data collection, fewer failed requests and clean price history. The post How to monitor e-book prices without losing half your data to failed requests first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
A Kindle title that costs $9.99 on amazon.com can sit at £4.99 on amazon.co.uk and 549 rupees on amazon.in on the same afternoon. Kobo runs promotions per storefront. Apple Books applies its own regional price tiers. If you are tracking a catalogue of even 2,000 titles across five storefronts, you are looking at roughly 10,000 price points per pass, and the moment your collector starts hammering a retailer from one address, the numbers you get back stop being trustworthy long before you get an outright error.

That is the real failure mode. Not a 403 page you can see and retry, but a 200 OK response containing a default-currency page, a cached price from four days ago, or a “temporarily unavailable” block where the buy box should be. Publishers and comparison sites that monitor e-book prices carelessly end up with clean-looking CSVs full of quiet nonsense.

What actually changes an e-book price

E-book pricing moves for three reasons, and they need different sampling rates. Publisher-set changes under agency terms propagate to every storefront at once and are relatively rare, often tied to a new release or a series promotion. Retailer-led discounting is faster: Amazon price-matches competitors algorithmically, so a Kobo daily deal can pull the Kindle price down within hours. Then there are scheduled promotions such as Kindle Monthly Deals or Kobo VIP sales, which start and end on known dates but with unannounced participants.

For most catalogues, a six-hour interval on active titles and a daily pass on the long tail is a sensible baseline. Hourly polling on 50,000 ASINs mostly generates load, not information.

Choosing a collection method before you choose infrastructure

Three routes exist, and picking the wrong one is the most expensive mistake in a price monitoring project. Official APIs are the cleanest but the most restricted. Affiliate feeds are permitted and cheap but incomplete. Direct page collection is the most complete and the most fragile.

Method Coverage Practical constraint When it makes sense
Amazon Product Advertising API 5.0 Kindle price, ASIN, availability Requires an approved associate account with qualifying sales; request quota scales with revenue, so new accounts are throttled hard You already run affiliate traffic and monitor under ~5,000 ASINs
Retailer affiliate feeds (Kobo, Apple Books via PHG) Catalogue-level pricing, refreshed daily Feed latency of 12-24 hours; short flash promotions are often missed entirely Long-tail catalogue baselines and metadata enrichment
Direct HTML collection Every storefront, every currency, promo badges, strike-through prices Per-region addressing required; response validation is on you; layout changes break parsers Competitive monitoring, multi-region price audits, promo detection
Third-party aggregators Whatever they cover, normalised Typically $0.002-0.01 per record, no control over refresh timing Small catalogues where engineering time costs more than data

Why direct collection needs per-region addressing

Storefronts localise on more than the domain. Amazon resolves a customer’s market from a combination of the domain, the session cookie and the requesting address, and it will happily serve a US-priced page from amazon.co.uk if it decides that is where you belong. Kobo redirects between storefronts on the same basis. Apple Books returns different price tiers per country. Collecting German prices from a Frankfurt address is not an optimisation, it is the only way to know the number is real.

Building a validation layer that catches silent errors

Before any address rotation or scheduling work, write the validator. It is the single highest-return component in a price monitoring stack and it takes an afternoon.

Check that the currency symbol matches the expected storefront, that the price falls inside a plausible band for the format (a Kindle edition at $0.00 is usually a Prime Reading badge parsed as a price, not a free book), that the ASIN or ISBN in the response matches the one you requested, and that the page contains the localised delivery or format string you expect. Anything failing validation goes to a retry queue with a different exit address, not into your database.

In practice a well-configured collector on a major retailer will show a single-digit percentage of validation failures. If you are seeing 30% or more, the problem is almost never the parser.

Address reputation is the variable most teams ignore

The technical difference between a collection run that returns 97% usable records and one that returns 60% is rarely bandwidth. It is who used the address before you. Datacenter ranges get recycled, and a subnet that was used for aggressive collection last quarter carries that history into your requests today.

There are four practical categories, and they are not interchangeable:

Shared datacenter addresses are the cheapest option and are adequate for smaller retailers, publisher sites and Google Play Books, but they are the first thing large storefronts filter. Dedicated datacenter addresses cost slightly more and behave far more predictably because you own the request history. Residential addresses carry the highest trust and matter most on Amazon and Apple, where consumer-network origin is part of the trust signal. Mobile addresses are the most expensive per unit and are rarely justified for e-book price collection, since book retailers do not apply the aggressive mobile-first checks that social platforms do.

Comparing providers on the dimensions that matter for price monitoring

Vendor comparisons usually rank on price per gigabyte, which is the wrong metric here. Price monitoring is a request-count workload with tiny payloads. A product page is 200-400 KB, so 10,000 checks is roughly 3 GB. Under bandwidth billing that is trivial; under per-address billing it is trivial too. What actually differs is location granularity, session persistence and whether you can hold the same address long enough to build a stable request history.

Provider Billing model Entry cost Fit for e-book price monitoring
proxys.io Per address, per month From $0.67 shared, $1.40-1.47 dedicated, $3.60 residential Strong for fixed-schedule multi-region collection; static addresses build stable history. Residential pool is narrow (Russia, Poland), so US residential needs a second source
Bright Data Per GB, residential pool Roughly $5-8 per GB at entry tiers Widest geo coverage and city-level targeting; overkill and expensive for a 10,000-request daily job
Oxylabs Per GB or per address Comparable to Bright Data, enterprise-oriented Good scraping APIs with built-in parsing; minimum commitments make small catalogues uneconomical
Decodo (formerly Smartproxy) Per GB, tiered Mid-market, lower entry commitment Reasonable middle ground; session control is good, per-country pool depth varies outside Tier 1
IPRoyal Per address or per GB Low entry cost on datacenter Cheap datacenter capacity; residential quality is inconsistent across regions

Prices above are published list rates and change; treat them as an order of magnitude, not a quote. The structural point holds regardless: if your workload is a predictable number of requests to a predictable set of storefronts on a schedule, per-address monthly billing is cheaper and more stable than per-gigabyte billing, and you get the added benefit of a request history that does not reset every session.

Scheduling and request shaping

Concurrency matters less than distribution. Twelve requests per second from one address looks like automation. The same volume spread across 40 addresses with randomised intervals between 800 ms and 3,000 ms looks like traffic. Keep per-address rates conservative, roughly one request every two to four seconds on major storefronts, and scale by adding addresses rather than by turning up the rate.

Two details that save time later. First, pin an address to a storefront for the whole run instead of rotating mid-session, because a session that changes country halfway through will get a redirect and your parser will record the wrong currency. Second, stagger collection windows across storefronts so European and North American passes do not both land at local peak, when response times climb and timeouts spike.

Latency is worth measuring but not obsessing over. A 400 ms round trip to a UK endpoint from a UK address is fine for a batch job that runs overnight. It matters only if you are trying to detect a flash sale within minutes of it starting, and very few catalogues justify that.

Where this breaks

Three limitations are worth stating plainly. Publisher-set agency pricing means a lot of collected variance is currency conversion noise rather than real competitive movement, so normalise to a single currency at the day’s rate before you compare anything. Subscription-inclusive titles distort averages badly, because a book included in Kindle Unlimited or Kobo Plus shows a nominal purchase price that almost nobody pays. And storefront layouts change without notice, so a parser that worked for eight months will fail on a Tuesday. Budget maintenance time, not just infrastructure.

There is also a legal boundary. Collecting publicly displayed prices for market research is generally defensible, but retailer terms of service and local rules differ, and none of this is legal advice. If the data feeds a commercial product, get it reviewed.

Practical starting configuration

For a catalogue of 2,000 to 5,000 titles across five storefronts, start with two dedicated addresses per target country, a six-hour cycle on the top 20% of titles by sales rank and a daily cycle on the rest, and a validation layer that rejects any record where currency, identifier and price band do not agree. At roughly $1.47 per address per month, ten addresses across five markets costs under $15 monthly, which is less than a single hour of the engineering time you will otherwise spend cleaning bad records.

Location coverage matters more than raw count when you are working across markets. The available address locations and pricing at proxys.io cover the storefronts that account for most English-language e-book revenue, including the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Netherlands, Spain, Poland, India and Canada.

Measure the result the way you would measure any pipeline: usable records per run, validation failure rate by storefront, and cost per 1,000 verified price points. If the third number climbs while the first two hold, you are paying for capacity you are not using. If validation failures climb on one storefront while others hold steady, replace the addresses assigned to that storefront before you touch the parser.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: First Look at the Meebook E6 e-reader
entries.summary: For an unboxing and first-hand look at the physical page-turn buttons, bezel design, and user interface of the Meebook E6 watch this video. The post First Look at the Meebook E6 e-reader first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Meebook has just released its first new e-reader in a couple of years, called the Meebook E6. The Meebook E6 is a 6-inch E-Ink e-reader running Android 11, with physical page-turn buttons, a sharp 300 PPI display, and access to the Google Play Store.

The Meebook E6 features a 6-inch E-Ink screen with a resolution of 1448×1072 and 300 PPI. It has an adjustable front-lit display and a warm lighting system to read during the day or night. The industrial design of the unit has a recessed screen, physical page-turn buttons, and a matcha green color scheme; it has the same color as the base Kindle.

Under the hood is a Quad-core 1.8 GHz processor with 3 GB of RAM and 32 GB of internal storage. A MicroSD card slot supports memory cards up to 512 GB. Listen to podcasts, audiobooks, or music with the built-in speaker, or connect to Bluetooth 5.0 with wireless headphones or earbuds. Make voice calls or use communication apps via the microphone. Download firmware updates, use apps, or surf the web with Wi-Fi. It is powered by a 2200 mAh battery and weighs approximately 180–190 g.

It is running a pretty old version of Google Android, by e-reader standards: Android 11. Many flagship apps will be dropping support for this outdated OS, so bear that in mind if you do anything else but read with Kindle, Kobo, NOOK or read manga, comics, webtoons, magazines, or newspapers. If you want to load in your own e-books, the E6 supports EPUB, FB2, DJVU, PDF, TXT, DOC, DOCX, MOBI, CBE, CBZ, AZW3, and HTML.

entries.title: Amazon revises Product Page for Kindle Paperwhite Kids
entries.summary: The "Summer Edition" case is a newly released, official Amazon cover included as an option with the Kindle Paperwhite Kids bundle. The post Amazon revises Product Page for Kindle Paperwhite Kids first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon has made some adjustments to the product description page of the Kindle Paperwhite for Kids on the desktop version of the website in the United States. There is a new banner at the top that says, “This Kindle includes comprehension features for kids, including Word Wise and Vocabulary Builder that help kids learn new words and tackle more advanced books.” They have also added a new case that comes for free with purchase called Summer Edition.

Word Wise is a popular feature on Amazon Kindle devices and reading apps that automatically displays short, simple definitions or synonyms inline above difficult or uncommon words while you read. It helps children, students, and English language learners understand challenging vocabulary without breaking their reading flow.

The “Summer Edition” case is a newly released, official Amazon cover included as an option with the Kindle Paperwhite Kids bundle. It is designed specifically to appeal to younger readers—and adults buying the kids’ bundle for the value—by embracing a seasonal, vibrant aesthetic.

entries.title: New Odyssey movie is driving people towards the audiobooks
entries.summary: Listens jumped more than 500% on the exact day the film premiered in cinemas. Gen Z accounts for 36% of the listening audience, and Millennials make up 45%. The post New Odyssey movie is driving people towards the audiobooks first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey is a mythic action epic adapting Homer’s foundational Greek saga. The three-hour film grossed $263.7 million worldwide in its opening weekend and was shot entirely with brand-new IMAX 70mm film. The movie is obviously such a success that it is driving people towards listening to the audiobook.

Homer’s epic poem The Odyssey has experienced a massive surge in audiobook popularity, jumping over 500% following the release of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation, with strong engagement from Gen Z listeners on platforms like Spotify and Audible.

Variety can exclusively reveal that the Nolan bump has extended to Spotify streams of the audiobook format of “The Odyssey.” According to Spotify, “Across 91 audiobook editions in 10 languages, ‘The Odyssey’ has now been listened to on Spotify for the equivalent of more than 43 years of continuous playback.”

Listens jumped more than 500% on the exact day the film premiered in cinemas. Gen Z accounts for 36% of the listening audience and Millennials make up 45%, bringing the average listener age down to 35. Roughly two-thirds of the audiobook listeners are male, an unusually high male-to-female ratio for classic literature on Spotify UK. Total print and book sales across all editions spiked 76% according to Circana BookScan, heavily favoring Emily Wilson’s 2017 modern translation.

Popular Audiobook Narrators & Versions

Ian McKellen: Narrates the celebrated Robert Fagles translation, offering a grand, dramatic delivery.

Claire Danes: Narrates Emily Wilson’s modern, accessible 2017 translation.

Dan Stevens: Brings Robert Fitzgerald’s lyrical and poetic translation to life.

Stephen Fry: Reads his own engaging, witty retelling of Odyssey: The Greek Myths Reimagined.

Benedict Cumberbatch & Full Cast: Features in the popular BBC Radio 4 dramatization.

entries.title: Apple TV+ debuts Neuromancer Trailer
entries.summary: Apple’s highly anticipated television adaptation of William Gibson’s genre-defining 1984 cyberpunk novel, Neuromancer, will officially premiere on January 22, 2027. The post Apple TV+ debuts Neuromancer Trailer first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Apple is doing a television series on the seminal book by William Gibson called Neuromancer. The book is a famous 1984 science fiction novel that created the cyberpunk genre. It follows a washed-up computer hacker named Case who is hired by a powerful artificial intelligence to pull off a dangerous corporate heist.

Apple TV+ unveiled the very first official teaser trailer and promotional artwork for the 10-episode sci-fi series at San Diego Comic-Con. The show will launch with its first two episodes in January 2027, followed by a weekly release schedule concluding on March 19, 2027.

“Neuromancer” is produced by Paramount Television Studios and Anonymous Content. Anonymous Content and Apple TV previously collaborated on “The Savant,” “Disclaimer” and “Defending Jacob.”

It’s a good sign that Gibson, who is one of the show’s executive producers, seems to be happy with how it turned out. Sharing the teaser on Bluesky, the author posted, “Anyone who doesn’t see how very satisfied I’ve been throughout production doesn’t get what I most want out of an adaptation. Mind you, that does tend to happen.”

Neuromancer (Sprawl Trilogy Book 1)
